earlier_scan.note: Extinct, essentially unattested (Glottolog lists no references; unclassifiable); no stress data can exist.

sources.note: Classification: Unclassifiable; AES status 10 (Extinct); NOCODE; zero bibliographic references listed.

Describes it as an extinct Northern Iroquoian language 'mutually intelligible with the Wendat language' (unsourced beyond Julian 2010); no vocabulary or grammatical data; only source cited is Julian 2010 for the ethnonym etymology.

sources.citation: Julian, Charles (2010). A History of the Iroquoian Languages. PhD thesis, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg. Section 18.3 'Wenro', pp. 336-337 (intro to ch. 18 p. 335).
sources.note: Nothing. Wenro is listed among the 'fragmentary (or altogether unattested) Northern Iroquoian languages' (p. 335); the Wenro section (pp. 336-337) is purely ethnohistorical: the only linguistic material is the Huron exonym <8enro'ronon>/<Ahouenrochrhonon> and the village name/ethnonym <Ouaroronon> recorded by La Roche Daillon in 1627. No Wenro words, phonology, or stress.

sources.citation: Hawkins, Alicia L. 2001. "Genoa Frilled Pottery and the Problem of the Identification of the Wenro in Huronia." Ontario Archaeology 72: 15-37.
sources.note: No language data. Useful negative evidence: 'The Jesuit Relations are the only primary sources referring to the Wenro by name'; the Wenro are described there only as 'an Iroquoian-speaking group politically allied with the Huron' and former allies of the Neutral; reviews Hewitt 1910 / White 1978 / Steckley 1982, 1985 etymologies of the name.

sources.citation: Mithun, Marianne. 1999. The Languages of Native North America (Cambridge Language Surveys). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Iroquoian family, pp. 418-424 (Wenro: pp. 419, 423).
sources.note: No phonology content for Wenro. p. 419: ".. languages thought to be Iroquoian are mentioned in historical accounts, but lack of attestation makes them impossible to classify precisely. These include Meherrin in the Southeast, and Erie, Wenro, Neutral, and Petun in western New York and Ontario." p. 423: "Immediately to the east were the Wenro, reported by the missionary Le Jeune to have spoken Neutral (Thwaites 1896-1901: 16.253)."

sources.citation: Garrad, Charles. 1998. "The Survival of the Wenro and How I Became One." KEWA (Newsletter of the London Chapter, Ontario Archaeological Society) 98-4 (Summer 1998), lead article (issue ISSN 0228-4111).
sources.note: No phonology content and no Wenro word forms. Ethnohistory + archaeology (Genoa Frilled pottery) + Steckley's etymology of the ethnonym. The only language remarks are second-hand: 'the opportunity afforded to learn the Neutral dialect spoken by the Wenros (JR16:253)'; 'Although it was by familiarising themselves with the Wenro dialect that two Jesuits from Huronia adept at languages were enabled to go to the Neutrals (JR21:187-9), the Wenros themselves were never again mentioned in Huronia'; Chaumonot called 'the Wenro/Neutral language specialist'; Barbeau 1915's Wyandot word for the Big Turt…

sources.citation: Steckley, John. 1985. "Why did the Wenro Turn Turtle?" Arch Notes (Newsletter of the Ontario Archaeological Society) 85(3): 17-19.
sources.note: No phonology content. Reanalyses Hewitt's 1910 etymology: Huron -wenr- 'moss' + -o- 'to be in water' + -ronnon 'people' ('people of the place of floating scum') vs. Steckley's proposal linking the name to Wyandot 'moss-backed turtle' (-wenr- + -ori- 'be covered'), i.e. the Wenro as the 'Turtle' nation adopted into the Huron Turtle clan in 1638.
sources.venue: Arch Notes (Newsletter of the Ontario Archaeological Society)

sources.citation: Mithun, Marianne. 1979. "Iroquoian." In Lyle Campbell & Marianne Mithun (eds.), The Languages of Native America: Historical and Comparative Assessment, pp. 133-212 (section 1.8 'Wenro', pp. 145-146). Austin: University of Texas Press.
sources.note: No phonology content. Verbatim (pp. 145-146, stitched from the archive.org full-text index): "1.8. Wenro. The Wenro language is also undocumented. According to Père Le Jeune (Thwaites 1896-1901:16-253) the Wenros, who were part of the Neutral Confederacy until 1637, spoke Neutral. During the early seventeenth century, the Wenros (Ahouenrochrhonons=Awerherhonons=Wenrohronons=Weanohronons=.."; and earlier: '.. scanty documentation. These include Petun, Neutral, Wenro, Erie, and Andaste or Susquehanna.'

sources.citation: Lounsbury, Floyd G. 1978. "Iroquoian Languages." In Bruce G. Trigger (ed.), Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 15: Northeast, pp. 334-343. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution.
sources.note: No phonology content for Wenro. The chapter's explicit classification (c. p. 335, after the Neutral name Attiwendaronk 'they (who) understand the language'): "For the Wenro and the Erie, on the other hand, nothing can be said about their linguistic relationships except that they certainly spoke Northern Iroquoian languages." (verbatim from archive.org full-text index of the lending scan).

sources.citation: Hewitt, J.N.B. 1910. "Wenrohronon." In Frederick Webb Hodge (ed.), Handbook of American Indians North of Mexico (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 30), part 2, pp. 932-934. Washington: Government Printing Office. (= the 'Hewitt 1912, p. 933' reprint cited in our bibliography via Julian 2010)
sources.note: No phonology content and no Wenro words. Gives a Huron etymology of the name (noun 'scum, moss, lather' + verb stem -o- 'to float / be immersed or contained in liquid' + tribal suffix -ronnon: 'the people or tribe of the place of floating scum', linked to the Cuba, N.Y. oil spring) and ethnohistory from the Jesuit Relations (association with the Neutral Nation, 1639 migration of 600+ to Huronia, population estimate 1,200-2,000).
sources.venue: Handbook of American Indians North of Mexico (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 30), part 2

sources.citation: Thwaites, Reuben Gold (ed.). 1898. The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, vol. XVI: Québec and Hurons, 1639, pp. 252-253 (French original and English translation of Le Jeune's Relation of 1639, Huron report by Jérôme Lalemant) and note 15. Cleveland: Burrows Brothers.
sources.note: No language data at all — no Wenro word is recorded. The only linguistic information is the classification remark (French, p. 252): ".. de prendre l'occasion que Dieu nous enuoyoit à nostre porte, d'entrer en quelque nation de la langue des Neutres, par l'arriuée en ce païs des 8eanohronons, qui s'y sont refugiez, comme nous dirons cy-apres; lesquels faisoient vne des Nations associées à la Nation neutre." (Eng. p. 253: 'that of entering a nation of the Neutral language through the arrival in this country of the Weanohronons, who have taken refuge here.. and who formed one of the Nations alli…
